Why Some Blackjack Tables Pay 6:5 Instead of 3:2 — and What It Costs You

Published October 24, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Walk onto almost any casino floor and you'll find at least one blackjack table with a small, easy-to-miss line on the felt: "Blackjack Pays 6 to 5." It looks like a minor variation in the fine print. It isn't. That single payout change is one of the most expensive rule tweaks in the entire game, and it quietly turns one of the best bets on the floor into a noticeably worse one — without changing a single strategy decision you make.

In this guide

  1. What 3:2 and 6:5 actually mean
  2. The dollar cost, hand by hand
  3. How much it adds to the house edge
  4. Why these tables exist at all

  6. Is it ever reasonable to play one anyway

What 3:2 and 6:5 actually mean

When your first two cards total 21 — an ace plus a ten-value card — that's a natural blackjack, and it normally pays a bonus over a standard win. On a traditional table, a natural pays 3:2, meaning a $10 bet returns $15 in winnings (plus your original $10 back). On a 6:5 table, the same $10 bet returns only $12 in winnings for the identical hand. You made the same bet, got the same cards, played no differently at all, and still walked away with less money.

The ratio itself is the whole story here. 3:2 means you're paid one and a half times your bet; 6:5 means you're paid only one and one-fifth times your bet. Every other part of blackjack — hitting, standing, doubling, splitting, basic strategy — can stay completely identical between two tables, and the 6:5 table will still be meaningfully worse, purely because of this one payout line.

The dollar cost, hand by hand

The gap between the two payouts scales directly with your bet size. Here's what a natural blackjack is worth at each ratio, and how much it costs you to be playing at a 6:5 table instead of a 3:2 one:

Bet size3:2 payout6:5 payoutLost on this hand
$10$15.00$12.00$3.00
$25$37.50$30.00$7.50
$50$75.00$60.00$15.00
$100$150.00$120.00$30.00

The pattern is consistent: a 6:5 table pays you exactly 30% less on every single natural blackjack you're dealt, no matter the stake. That might sound like a one-time hit rather than an ongoing cost, but naturals aren't rare enough to ignore — a player gets dealt one roughly once every 20 to 21 hands on average. Over a few hours at the table, that adds up to a real, repeated discount on one of the best outcomes the game offers you.

How much it adds to the house edge

Blackjack played with correct basic strategy on a standard 3:2, decent-rules table typically carries a house edge around 0.5% — among the lowest of any casino game. Switching only the payout to 6:5 is widely calculated to add roughly 1.4 percentage points to that edge, pushing a game that was close to a coin flip up toward something closer to a 2% house edge overall.

You can see roughly where that number comes from without any advanced math. A natural comes up on about 4.8% of hands. Each time it does, a 6:5 table pays you 0.3 times your bet less than a 3:2 table would (the gap shown in the table above, as a fraction of your stake). Multiply the frequency by the size of the loss — about 4.8% of hands, each costing roughly 30% of a bet relative to 3:2 — and you land close to that same 1.4-percentage-point figure. It's a small-looking rule buried in the felt that does an outsized amount of damage to your expected results.

A 1.4-point swing might not sound dramatic, but it roughly triples a well-played blackjack hand's house edge from around 0.5% to something closer to 2% — undoing most of the reason blackjack has a reputation as one of the best bets in the casino.

Why these tables exist at all

Casinos didn't invent the 6:5 payout to be sneaky in a vacuum — it's a direct response to pressure on their margins from other directions. Single-deck and double-deck games are easier for skilled players to track and count, so casinos use the weaker payout as a built-in compensator that keeps the game profitable even on low-deck-count tables where counting is more viable. It also shows up often on tables with continuous shuffling machines and on lower-minimum, high-volume tables where the casino is prioritizing speed and throughput over the traditional full-shoe game.

In short: 6:5 tables tend to cluster around exactly the conditions — fewer decks, faster shuffling, lower minimums — that would otherwise be more favorable to players, which is part of why the trade-off can be easy to miss if you're only looking at the deck count or the table minimum.

How to spot one before you sit down

The payout ratio is required to be posted on the table, usually printed directly on the felt near the betting circles or on a small placard. Before you sit down, look for the phrase "Blackjack Pays 3 to 2" or "Blackjack Pays 6 to 5" — it's almost always visible without needing to ask a dealer. If a table doesn't show the ratio clearly, or you're unsure, it's reasonable to ask the dealer directly; they're required to tell you.

  • Single and double-deck tables carry 6:5 payouts more often than 6-deck shoe games, precisely because fewer decks would otherwise favor skilled players more.
  • Lower-minimum tables (particularly $5–$15 minimums in busy casinos) are disproportionately likely to run 6:5, since the casino is optimizing for volume rather than game quality.
  • Online and live-dealer tables vary by operator and by specific game title — check the payout line in the game's rules or paytable before playing, the same way you would on a physical table.

Is it ever reasonable to play one anyway

Sometimes. If a 6:5 table is the only option at a stake you're comfortable with, or the alternative is a much higher minimum you don't want to play, it's not an irrational choice — it's a trade-off, and you're allowed to value convenience, table atmosphere, or a lower minimum over squeezing out the best possible odds. The point of knowing the math isn't that you're obligated to avoid every 6:5 table; it's that you should know what you're giving up so the choice is informed rather than accidental. For most players optimizing purely for the odds, though, hunting down a 3:2 table at a similar minimum is one of the single highest-value adjustments available in casino gambling — bigger than any amount of basic strategy fine-tuning. Pair that search with our guide to blackjack basic strategy and our broader look at house edge across casino games to get the full picture of where your money actually goes.

Frequently asked questions

Does basic strategy change on a 6:5 table?

No. The correct play for every hand is identical on 6:5 and 3:2 tables — hitting, standing, doubling, and splitting decisions don't change. Only the payout for a natural blackjack changes, which is exactly why the cost is so easy to overlook.

Are there payout ratios worse than 6:5?

Yes, though they're less common. Some novelty or specialty blackjack variants have used even weaker ratios like 1:1 (even money) on a natural. Always check the posted payout before playing, regardless of how familiar the game looks.

Is a 6-deck 3:2 table always better than a single-deck 6:5 table?

In terms of pure house edge, usually yes — the payout difference tends to outweigh what you gain from fewer decks unless you're an experienced card counter who can actually exploit the lower deck count, which the casino is specifically pricing against with the weaker payout.

Do online casinos use 6:5 payouts too?

Some do, on specific game titles, though standard 3:2 remains common for mainstream online and live-dealer blackjack. The payout ratio is listed in the game's rules or info screen — it's worth checking before you start playing any new title.

Can side bets make up for a 6:5 payout?

No — side bets like Perfect Pairs or 21+3 carry their own, typically much higher house edge and are priced independently of the main game. Adding a side bet to a 6:5 table increases your overall edge against you rather than offsetting it.
